# Primary sclerosing cholangitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the gallbladder and biliary tract > Primary sclerosing cholangitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/nS07Zf)

---

## Summary

Primary <u>sclerosing</u> <u>cholangitis</u> (PSC) is a progressive <u>chronic inflammation</u> of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts. The exact etiology is unknown but there is a strong association with autoimmune diseases, particularly <u>ulcerative colitis</u> (UC). In the early stages, PSC is often asymptomatic. As the disease progresses, patients may present with <u>right upper quadrant</u> abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>pruritus</u>, fatigue, and weight loss. Laboratory tests show findings of <u>cholestasis</u>, including elevated <u>alkaline phosphatase</u> (<u>ALP</u>) and <u>gamma-glutamyltransferase</u> (<u>GGT</u>). While not recommended for diagnosis, <u>pANCA</u> is positive in up to 80% of cases. <u>Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography</u> (<u>MRCP</u>) or <u>endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography</u> (<u>ERCP</u>) is used for diagnostic confirmation. Management is primarily symptomatic, with <u>liver transplantation</u> reserved for <u>end-stage liver disease</u>.




![Overview of PSC, PBC, and autoimmune hepatitis](media/vjhjwjul5ms1144omhpvm3uy.jpg)

## Epidemiology

* Sex: : <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (2:1)

* Age: : The median age at diagnosis is ∼ 40.





References:[[1]](/library/zj0r1T)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* The exact cause is unknown.

* Associations

* <u>Chronic inflammatory bowel diseases</u> (<u>IBD</u>)

* ∼ 90% of patients with PSC have <u>IBD</u> (approx. 87% of these patients have <u>ulcerative colitis</u>) and ∼ 13% have <u>Crohn disease</u>.

* However, only approx. 5% of patients with UC and < 5% of patients with <u>Crohn disease</u> develop PSC.

* Presence of <u>HLA-B8</u> and <u>HLA-DR3</u>

* Other autoimmune conditions (e.g., <u>hypergammaglobulinemia</u> <u>IgM</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> The majority of patients with PSC also have <u>ulcerative colitis</u>.References:[[1]](/library/zj0r1T)[[2]](/library/-j0D1T)

---

## Clinical features

* Often initially asymptomatic

* Signs of <u>cholestasis</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u>/<u>scleral icterus</u>

* <u>Pruritus</u>

* Pale stool, dark urine

* Fatigue

* Can lead to <u>acute cholangitis</u> (<u>fever</u>, chills, <u>right upper quadrant</u> <u>pain</u>)

* Later stages: signs of <u>cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* <u>Portal hypertension</u>

* <u>Liver</u> failure

* Symptoms of chronic <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u>, which is frequently associated with PSC, or other associated comorbidities





References:[[2]](/library/-j0D1T)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)




* Suspect PSC in patients with persistently elevated <u>cholestatic enzymes</u>.

* Obtain abdominal imaging (e.g., <u>ultrasound</u>) to evaluate for <u>biliary obstruction</u>.

* Obtain further studies for diagnostic confirmation.

* No <u>biliary obstruction</u>: <u>MRCP</u>

* <u>Biliary obstruction</u>: therapeutic <u>ERCP</u>

* Consider <u>liver biopsy</u> in select patients.





> [!TIP]
> The diagnosis of PSC is based on persistently elevated <u>cholestatic enzymes</u>, characteristic <u>bile duct strictures</u> seen on <u>MRCP</u> or <u>ERCP</u>, and the exclusion of <u>secondary sclerosing cholangitis</u>. [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[5]](/library/aycQdU0)




#### Routine studies




* <u>Cholestatic enzymes</u>

* ↑ <u>ALP</u>

* ↑ <u>GGT</u>

* Normal or ↑ <u>conjugated bilirubin</u>

* <u>Transaminases</u>: normal or moderately elevated (approx.  2–3× <u>ULN</u>) <u>AST</u> and <u>ALT</u>  [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)

* <u>Lipid profile</u>: ↑ total <u>cholesterol</u>  [[6]](/library/hyccUU0)

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>Thrombocytopenia</u> may be a sign of <u>cirrhosis</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> Suspect PSC in patients with a history of <u>inflammatory bowel disease</u> and elevated <u>cholestatic enzymes</u> (<u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>, and <u>conjugated bilirubin</u>).




#### <u>Serological studies</u>




Findings are typically nonspecific but may help support the diagnosis or differential diagnoses.




| <br><u>Serological studies</u> in patients with suspected PSC [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Autoantibodies</u> | <br><br>* Atypical <u>perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies</u> (<u>pANCA</u>): present in up to 80% of patients with PSC.<br><br>* <u>ANAs</u>: present in up to ∼ 75% of patients with PSC<br><br>* <u>ASMAs</u>: presence suggests <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Antimitochondrial antibodies</u>: presence supports <u>primary biliary cholangitis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Immunoglobulins</u> | <br><br>* <u>IgM</u>: elevated in ∼ 50% of patients with PSC<br><br>* <u>IgG</u>: elevated in ∼ 60% of patients with PSC<br><br>* IgG4: elevation suggests <u>IgG4-associated cholangitis</u>  [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> All patients should be tested for elevated IgG4 at least once, as findings may influence management. [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)




### Imaging [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[7]](/library/IKXY3_)




#### Initial imaging




Obtain abdominal imaging for all patients to evaluate for <u>biliary obstruction</u>.




* Modalities: <u>ultrasound</u>, <u>CT scan with contrast</u>, <u>MRI</u>

* Supportive findings

* Diffuse thickening of the <u>bile</u> duct walls

* Focal <u>bile</u> duct dilatations

* Possibly <u>gallbladder</u> abnormalities, e.g., thickening, enlargement





#### Advanced imaging




Obtain for all patients for diagnostic confirmation.




* <u>Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography</u> 

* Method of choice (if there is no <u>biliary obstruction</u>)

* Supportive findings: multifocal intrahepatic and extrahepatic <u>bile duct strictures</u> alternating with dilatation and beading of <u>bile</u> ducts

* <u>Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography</u> 

* Should not be used for diagnosis of PSC except in the following scenarios:

* Need for simultaneous therapeutic intervention for <u>biliary obstruction</u>

* <u>Contraindications to MRI</u>

* Supportive findings: similar to <u>MRCP</u>





![Sclerosing cholangitis in ulcerative colitis](media/phk3w9zsh56guls64mt29zyv.jpg)

Sclerosing cholangitis in ulcerative colitis

![ERCP in primary sclerosing cholangitis](media/rflia5g92j8u7024585as5w0.jpg)

ERCP in primary sclerosing cholangitis




### <u>Liver biopsy</u> [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)




* Not routinely indicated as part of the workup for PSC

* Consider in select patients to evaluate for:

* Small-duct PSC

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis-PSC overlap syndrome</u>

* Finding: concentric periductal onion <u>skin</u> <u>fibrosis</u> (typical but rare)

## Differential diagnoses

| Differential diagnoses of cholestatic biliary disease |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Primary <u>sclerosing</u> <u>cholangitis</u> | <u>Primary biliary cholangitis</u> | <br><u>Secondary sclerosing cholangitis</u> [[8]](/library/eaXxj9)[[9]](/library/UaXbP9)<br> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br>* More common among middle-aged men<br><br> | <br>* More common among middle-aged women<br><br> | <br>* Depends on the underlying condition<br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br>* Progressive <u>chronic inflammation</u> of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts<br><br> | <br>* Progressive destruction of only intrahepatic small and medium-sized <u>bile</u> ducts<br><br> | <br><br>* Develops secondary to an underlying condition, including:<br><br>* Chronic <u>biliary obstruction</u> (e.g., stones, tumors, strictures)<br><br>* Trauma or <u>surgery</u> of the <u>biliary tract</u><br><br>* <u>Chronic pancreatitis</u><br><br>* <u>Ischemic</u> injury to the <u>biliary tract</u> (e.g., post-<u>transplantation</u>, critically ill patients)<br><br>* <u>Cholestasis</u> and elevated pressure in intrahepatic <u>bile</u> ducts lead to progressive <u>fibrosis</u> and eventually <u>cirrhosis</u><br><br><br> |
| Clinical presentation | <br><br>* <u>Pruritus</u><br><br>* Fatigue<br><br>* <u>Jaundice</u><br><br>* <u>Hepatomegaly</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Similar to PSC<br><br>* Potentially <u>xanthomas</u> and <u>xanthelasma</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Similar to PSC<br><br>* Additional symptoms corresponding to the underlying condition<br><br>* Poor prognosis<br><br><br> |
| Laboratory tests | <br><br>* <u>pANCA</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>, and <u>conjugated bilirubin</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Anti-<u>mitochondrial</u> <u>antibodies</u> (<u>AMA</u>)<br><br>* ↑ <u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>, and <u>conjugated bilirubin</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ <u>ALP</u>, <u>GGT</u>, and <u>conjugated bilirubin</u><br><br>* Additional changes corresponding to the underlying condition<br><br><br> |
| Associated conditions | <br>* <u>Ulcerative colitis</u> and <u>cholangiocarcinoma</u><br><br> | <br>* Autoimmune conditions<br><br> | <br>* May lead to <u>ascending cholangitis</u><br><br> |





![Primary sclerosing cholangitis vs. Primary biliary cholangitis](media/lf2syprsgd25fhgxaj9ev5ld.jpg)

The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Management

### General principles [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)




* Management is primarily supportive and includes:

* <u>Management of cholestasis-associated pruritus</u>, e.g., with <u>cholestyramine</u>

* Interventional treatment as needed to relieve obstructions

* Monitoring for commonly associated conditions and complications

* No medications currently prevent disease progression (e.g., reduced time to <u>liver transplantation</u>). [[10]](/library/E118if0)

* <u>Liver transplantation</u> is the only curative treatment but has a significant risk of disease recurrence.





### Pharmacological management [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[5]](/library/aycQdU0)




* <u>Ursodeoxycholic acid</u> (<u>UDCA</u>)

* Widely used, but evidence of benefit is mixed.  [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)

* May decrease <u>transaminases</u>, <u>ALP</u>, and serum <u>bilirubin</u>

* <u>Immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>); usually reserved for patients with overlap syndromes: [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)

* <u>IgG4-associated cholangitis</u>

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis-PSC overlap syndrome</u>





### Interventional treatment [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[5]](/library/aycQdU0)




Perform as needed in patients with relevant strictures. [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)




* <u>ERCP</u> with dilation of stenoses

* Indications

* To relieve symptoms caused by stenosis, e.g., <u>pruritus</u> and/or <u>cholangitis</u>

* To exclude <u>cholangiocarcinoma</u>

* <u>Stenting</u> may be necessary for severe strictures.

* Provide prophylactic <u>antibiotics</u> to prevent post-<u>ERCP</u> <u>cholangitis</u> .

* Percutaneous <u>cholangiography</u>

* Indication: patients who cannot undergo <u>ERCP</u>

* Requires placement of a percutaneous drain





> [!TIP]
> Patients with PSC are at increased risk for post-<u>ERCP</u> <u>cholangitis</u>. [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)




### <u>Liver transplantation</u> [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[11]](/library/WycPVU0)




* Refer patients with <u>decompensated cirrhosis</u> and a <u>MELD score</u> > 14.

* Additional <u>MELD</u> points may be offered to patients with:

* Recurrent <u>cholangitis</u> with recurrent <u>bacteremia</u> (> 2 episodes) or <u>sepsis</u> (> 1 episode)

* <u>Cholangiocarcinoma</u> < 3 cm in diameter without <u>metastasis</u>

* Intractable <u>pruritus</u>





### Screening and monitoring [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[7]](/library/IKXY3_)




Patients with PSC are at increased risk of <u>IBD</u>, progression of <u>liver</u> disease to <u>cirrhosis</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>,  and <u>malignancy</u>.




| <br>Screening and monitoring of complications and comorbidities in PSC [[3]](/library/5F1iii0)[[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[7]](/library/IKXY3_)<br> |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |  | Modalities | Timing |
| <u>Inflammatory bowel disease</u> |  |  |  |  | <br>* <u>Ileocolonoscopy</u><br><br> | <br>* At time of PSC diagnosis, then:<br><br>* Every 1–2 years in patients with <u>IBD</u><br><br>* Consider every 3–5 years in patients without <u>IBD</u>. [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)<br><br> |
| <u>Colorectal carcinoma</u> |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| <u>Cholangiocarcinoma</u> |  |  |  |  | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u><br><br>* Possibly serum <u>CA 19-9</u> measurements  [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Annually<br><br> |
| <u>Gallbladder carcinoma</u> |  |  |  |  | <br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u><br><br> | <br>* Annually<br><br> |
| Progression of <u>liver</u> disease |  |  |  |  | <br><br>* <u>Liver chemistries</u><br><br>* <u>Coagulation studies</u><br><br>* <u>Fibrosis</u> staging with <u>transient elastography</u> or <u>MR elastography</u><br><br>* Screening for <u>fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Obtain at diagnosis then regularly.<br><br> |
| <u>Osteoporosis</u> |  |  |  |  | <br>* <u>BMD testing</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Screening for osteoporosis</u> at PSC diagnosis and every 2–4 years thereafter  [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[11]](/library/WycPVU0)<br><br> |
| <br><u>Complications of cirrhosis</u> [[12]](/library/SycyeU0)<br> |  |  |  | <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u> | <br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>.<br><br> | <br>* Every 6 months<br><br> |
| <u>Esophageal varices</u> | <br>* <u>EGD</u><br><br> | <br><br>* At <u>cirrhosis</u> diagnosis<br><br>* Then every 2–3 years<br><br><br> |  |  |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> Patients with both PSC and UC have a 4–5 times higher risk of developing colorectal <u>dysplasia</u> or cancer than those with UC alone. [[4]](/library/BBcz1U0)[[11]](/library/WycPVU0)

---

## Complications

* <u>Steatorrhea</u> and <u>deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins</u>

* <u>Liver cirrhosis</u>

* <u>Bacterial cholangitis</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* <u>Cholangiocarcinoma</u> (∼ 10–15% of cases) [[7]](/library/IKXY3_)

* <u>Gallbladder carcinoma</u>

* <u>Colorectal carcinoma</u>  [[7]](/library/IKXY3_)[[13]](/library/rKXf3_)

* <u>Hepatocellular carcinoma</u> [[7]](/library/IKXY3_)

* <u>Pancreatic carcinoma</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
